hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever tried meditating and felt like you were bad at it?
options: then this story is for you. a monk almost gave up too.
then you’ll love what the buddha tells him.
perfect. you’ll start with the right idea.

steps.line: In ancient India, a young Buddhist monk named Sona practiced in a quiet forest grove. He pushed himself harder than anyone, day and night.
But his mind would not settle. Alone, he thought: I try harder than everyone, and it isn’t working. Maybe I should go home.

steps.q: The Buddha comes to Sona. What do you think he does?
o: Tells him to try even harder
Asks about his life before he was a monk
Tells him to rest for a few days
steps.why: He asks about Sona’s old life. Before he became a monk, Sona played the lute.

steps.line: The Buddha came and sat with him. Before you were a monk, he asked, you played the lute, didn’t you? Yes, said Sona.
When the strings were too tight, did it sound good? No, said Sona. And when they were too loose? No.

steps.q: Why ask a struggling monk about lute strings?
o: Effort is like a string: it needs tuning
To cheer him up with memories of home
To hint he’d be happier home with music
steps.why: Sona was straining like an over-tight string. The fix wasn’t to quit. It was better tuning.

steps.line: And neither too tight nor too loose? Beautiful. Effort is the same, said the Buddha. Too much makes you restless. Too little makes you lazy. Keep it balanced.

steps.q: Before the Buddha came, Sona had pushed so hard that something happened. What?
o: His feet bled on the walking path
He lost his voice from chanting
steps.why: The old account says he walked meditation until his feet bled. The same account says he was so delicate that hair grew on the soles of his feet.

steps.line: Sona tuned his effort, and in time he woke up fully. Today, meditation teachers still use his lute to explain how hard to try.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Match each string to what it looks like when you meditate.
pairs: forcing your mind to go blank
drifting off and never coming back
steps.why: The noticing isn’t failure. It’s the tuned string. Every time you come back is one more note.

say: here’s what i love. the buddha didn’t tell sona to want less. he told him to tune.
in buddhist teaching, you rest your attention on the breath. the mind wanders. you notice, and come back, without forcing. no blank mind required.

steps.q: A friend says, “I meditated for one minute and my mind wandered ten times. I’m terrible at this.” What would the Buddha’s lute lesson say?
o: They should quit and try something else
They should squeeze harder until the thoughts stop
Coming back ten times is the practice, gently tuned
steps.why: Ten wanders means ten returns. Forcing the thoughts out is the too-tight string.

today.say: try one tuned breath today. breathe in, let it out a little longer. if a thought shows up, notice it and finish the breath.
options: that’s one note on a tuned string.
that counts. the string will wait for you.

tomorrow.line: the most powerful man in the world kept writing himself one reminder.

card.from: a story from the Buddhist suttas
card.keepWhy: Not too tight, not too loose.
sources: Anguttara Nikaya 6.55, Sona Sutta (Sona Kolivisa at Rajagaha, in the Cool Wood): Sona considers returning to lay life; the Buddha appears before him and asks about the lute strings too tight, too loose, and tuned; energy should be balanced. Sona later becomes an arahant. Trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Numerical Discourses of the Buddha (2012).
Breath meditation: Anapanasati Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 118.
check: The teach and today steps apply the lute lesson to breath meditation; the sutta is about effort in general (Sona was doing walking meditation). Confirm the bridge is fair.
